sections.h2: What does the Richland County Recorder of Deeds do?
sections.html:
The Richland County Recorder keeps the public record of who owns land in the county and which liens and mortgages sit on it. The counter is in the county building at 50 Park Avenue East, Mansfield. It opens on weekdays at 8:00 AM, closes at 4:00 PM, and takes no new filings after 3:45 PM. Call 419-774-5602.

The county's own recorder page traces the job back to 1787, when the Northwest Territory set up a recorder in every county. Statehood came in 1803, the job became an elected one in 1829, and a four-year term was fixed in 1936. Each filing is indexed so a title examiner can trace ownership from one holder to the next. The county page adds that the recorder answers to more than 1,000 sections of state law.

For a seller in Richland County, the recorder is the last stop. Once the buyer's deed is recorded, the transfer becomes part of the public record.

sections.h2: What are the steps to record a Richland County deed?
sections.html:
Deeds pass through several county offices before they are recorded. A typical sequence looks like this.

  • Sign and acknowledge the deed. Sign the deed, then acknowledge the signature before an officer section 5301.01 allows: a notary, a judge, a court clerk, the county auditor or engineer, or a mayor.
  • Request tax map pre-approval by email to taxmap@richlandcountyoh.gov. The recorder's page says pre-approval must be included with any electronic deed transfer for real estate.
  • At the Auditor's counter, file the conveyance statement, pay the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax, and get the endorsement.
  • Hand the endorsed deed and the recording fee to the Recorder ahead of the 3:45 PM cutoff.

Electronic deed transfers are accepted. Anything the Tax Map Office and the Auditor must review still has to be carried to the courthouse. Staff do not hand out legal forms and point people to an attorney for drafting help.

sections.h2: Why does the Richland County Tax Map Office look at my deed?
sections.html:
The Tax Map Office is a division of the Richland County Engineer's Office, and it keeps the property map for every deeded parcel for the auditor. Its services include checking all recorded deeds, maintaining current maps with ownership, providing copies of surveys and checking surveys done in the county. Its collection of tax maps reaches back to 1853 and includes old road record books from the early 1800s. Phone 419-774-5620. The counter keeps the same weekday schedule as the rest of the building.

Because the office checks deeds against its maps, a seller who is splitting a lot or changing a legal description should raise it with tax map staff before the closing date.

sections.h2: What does the Auditor require before a deed is recorded in Richland County?
sections.html:
Section 319.202 requires the buyer or a representative to submit a statement of the property's value first. Only then does the auditor endorse the deed. The statement carries two affirmations. One asks whether the seller's bill carried a reduction such as homestead or owner occupancy. The other asks about CAUV farm valuation, since land that drops out can owe recoupment under section 5713.34.

The seller, as grantor, pays the conveyance fee set in section 319.54(G)(3). A commissioner-adopted transfer tax under Chapter 322 falls on the seller as well. The ceiling for that county tax is thirty cents per hundred dollars of value, and the auditor collects it when the deed is delivered, before recording. The Richland County Treasurer's page adds that conveyance fees are paid at the treasurer's office. Ask the Auditor what applies to your sale before setting a closing date.

The statute counts value as the whole consideration, any mortgage or vendor's lien included, and forbids willful misstatement.

sections.h2: What does Richland County charge to record a document?
sections.html:
Recording fees are set by Ohio law. Ohio's schedule starts with a seventeen dollar base fee and a seventeen dollar housing trust fund fee for the first two pages, and each added page carries four dollars of each. A preservation surcharge of up to five dollars is optional for counties (section 317.32). Certified copies and photocopies carry their own per-page charges under the same section.

Because page count moves the total, confirm the amount for your own document by phone. Use 419-774-5602 before sending any payment.

sections.h2: How do I search Richland County land records?
sections.html:
A link on the recorder's page opens an online records search where deeds, mortgages and releases can be read. This is useful for a seller checking whether an old mortgage was ever released, or whether a prior owner's lien is still on file.

The auditor's property search adds parcel data, and the Land Bank at 50 Park Avenue East, lower level 1, acquires vacant and abandoned properties. Heirs who plan to sell should check that the last recorded deed names the person who holds title.

sections.h2: Do older Richland County deeds without witnesses still count?
sections.html:
Usually yes. A deed signed before February 1, 2002 without the two witnesses the earlier law asked for is still deemed properly executed under section 5301.01(B), absent fraud in obtaining the signature. Recording it with the recorder of the land's county puts later buyers and lenders on notice.

The rule protects families holding old deeds. It does not fix a missing acknowledgment on a newly signed deed, so a current deed still needs the notary or other officer named in the statute.

sections.h2: Who decides whether Richland County charges a transfer tax?
sections.html: The board of county commissioners does. Under section 322.02, a county may levy a real property transfer tax by resolution, after two public hearings held three to ten days apart with newspaper, website or public notice sites carrying notice for two consecutive weeks. The resolution is subject to referendum unless adopted as an emergency measure by a unanimous vote. The commissioners may also send the question to voters, and then it takes effect only if a majority approves. The rate is a local choice, so a neighboring county's figure says nothing about Richland's.

sections.h2: What does the Richland County housing stock mean for deed work?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau counts 54,904 housing units and 124,893 residents for 2025, with 114 building permits issued that year. Median monthly owner costs are $1,218 where a mortgage exists and $489 where none does. Nearly nine in ten residents (87.6%) were in the same house a year earlier.

Land in Richland County stretches from Mansfield, Ontario and Shelby to villages such as Bellville, Lexington and Plymouth, and into townships named Springfield, Troy, Weller and Worthington.

faqs.q: Where is the Richland County Recorder located?
faqs.a: It is at 50 Park Avenue East in Mansfield, Ohio 44902, phone 419-774-5602. Filings stop at 3:45 PM on weekdays.

faqs.q: Is tax map approval needed before a Richland County deed is recorded?
faqs.a: Yes for electronic deed transfers. The recorder's page says tax map pre-approval must come with the deed and gives taxmap@richlandcountyoh.gov as the address to request it.

faqs.q: Can I record a Richland County deed online?
faqs.a: Partly. Electronic deed transfers are accepted, while documents needing Tax Map and Auditor review go in person. Call 419-774-5602 to confirm which route fits your document.

faqs.q: Which party covers the conveyance fee on a Richland County sale?
faqs.a: The grantor, meaning the seller. The seller, as grantor, owes it along with any county transfer tax, paid before recording.

faqs.q: Will the Richland County Recorder supply legal forms?
faqs.a: No. No. Staff say they do not supply legal forms and suggest asking an attorney.
